I have gathered extensive material. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes from what I've been able to read.

## Exodus 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter is widely understood as a "preview of the contest with Pharaoh" (Ex 5:1–6:1). Four episodes are identified: (a) the first encounter with Pharaoh (vv. 1–9), (b) the increased oppression (vv. 10–14), (c) the plea of the Israelite foremen (vv. 15–21), and (d) Moses' complaint (vv. 22–6:1). The enthusiasm of the worship in Exodus 4:31 turns sour when Pharaoh refuses, and the people encounter opposition rather than instant blessing. — Precept Austin (citing UBS and NET notes): https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-5-commentary

---

### v. 1 — "After that, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh… 'Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.'"

- **The courage of Moses and Aaron.** Pharaoh was considered a god—an inscription by one Pharaoh reads, "I am that which was, and is, and shall be, and no man has lifted my veil." Moses, having grown up in Pharaoh's courts, knew this well, yet with the authority of the living God he confronted him. — Enduring Word (David Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **"Let My people go."** God asserts that Israel belongs to Him, not Pharaoh. God's fundamental demand is freedom for His people. This command is repeated some nine times through the Exodus narrative (Ex 5:1; 7:16; 8:1, 20, 21; 9:1, 13; 10:3, 4). — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-5-commentary

- **The modest request.** God's entire purpose is not at once revealed. Pharaoh is tried with a moderate demand — a three-day feast in the wilderness — which he might well have granted. By refusing, he showed himself harsh, tempting God to lay a greater burden on him. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **The location of the court.** Ellicott identifies the court as being at Zoan (Tanis), the ordinary residence of Rameses II and his son Menephthah (citing Psalm 78:12, 43). — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **"In the wilderness"** — beyond inhabited Egypt — so that the Egyptians would not be driven to fury by seeing animals sacrificed which they regarded as sacred (cf. Exodus 8:26). — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Gill adds:** The demand was just — Israel was God's people, service was due to Him, and Pharaoh had no right to detain them. The entire dismissal is not at once demanded, but this small request was put in this form to try Pharaoh and make him inexcusable. — Gill (Baptist/Reformed): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

- **NET note:** The Hebrew verb translated "let go" (שַׁלַּח, shallakh) is a Piel imperative meaning "send away, release, dismiss, discharge." Jacob observes, "If a person was dismissed through the use of this verb, then he ceased to be within the power or sphere of influence of the individual who had dismissed him. He was completely free." — Precept Austin (citing NET): https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-5-commentary

- **Historical background on labour.** Constable cites Kenneth Kitchen's research showing that Egyptian royal workmen at Deir el-Medina routinely claimed time off for religious observances, "offering to his god," or "brewing for his feast." So Moses' request was not unprecedented; Pharaoh's reaction was almost, "Not another holiday!" — Precept Austin (citing Constable/Kitchen): https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-5-commentary

---

### v. 2 — "Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice… I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go."

- **Pharaoh's ignorance.** If Pharaoh really knew who the LORD was, he would have gladly released Israel. Pharaoh did not have the right heart, but he did ask the right question. — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **"Who is Jehovah?"** Ellicott notes that if the name Jehovah had fallen into disuse in the later chapters of Genesis and was revived at the burning bush, Pharaoh may genuinely not have heard of it. The Egyptians were accustomed to the idea of local gods whose power was circumscribed, not extending beyond the race or nation to which the god belonged. Pharaoh meant that Jehovah could have no authority over him since He was not one of Egypt's gods. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Pharaoh as a divine figure.** Pharaoh was not only king but considered a divine person. When Moses asked Pharaoh to accede to Yahweh's command, Pharaoh saw this as a threat to his sovereignty. — Constable (via Precept Austin): https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-5-commentary

- **Gill notes:** Pharaoh declares he knows of no superior monarch whose orders he was obliged to obey. The Targum of Jonathan paraphrases: "I have not found the name of Jehovah written in the book of angels, I am not afraid of him." — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** observes that Pharaoh's rejection of the knowledge and authority of Jehovah is "vital to the understanding of the hardening of Pharaoh's heart. The first step was Pharaoh's. He made a deliberate choice to reject the knowledge of God. This led to his ultimate fatal decline. Paul outlines this process in Romans 1:19-32." — Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-5.html

---

### v. 3 — "The God of the Hebrews has met with us… Please let us go on a three-day journey… to sacrifice to the LORD our God, or He may strike us with plagues or with the sword."

- **A softer approach.** Moses accepts Pharaoh's view and does not insist on the authority of Jehovah over Egyptians. Instead, he makes an appeal *ad misericordiam*: God has authority over Hebrews and will be angered if they neglect His requirement. Will Pharaoh not allow them to escape His anger? — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **"With the sword."** Egypt was open to invasion on its eastern frontier, and the brunt of an invasion would fall upon the Hebrews. In the time of the nineteenth dynasty, Hittite incursions were especially feared. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Constable** notes that in this second appeal, Moses and Aaron used milder terms — they presented themselves not as ambassadors of Yahweh but as representatives of their brethren, did not mention the name "Yahweh" (unknown to Pharaoh) or "Israel" (which would have struck him as arrogant), did not command but requested ("Please…"), and gave reasons. — Constable (via Precept Austin): https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-5-commentary

- **Gill:** They also suggest that should they be smitten with pestilence or sword, Pharaoh would lose the benefit of their bond-service — a considerable decline in his revenues. — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

---

### vv. 4–5 — "Moses and Aaron, why do you draw the people away from their work? Get back to your labor! … the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor."

- **Pharaoh's counter-attack.** Pharaoh not only rejected giving the Israelites time off; he saw the request itself as a waste of good working time. He accused Moses and Aaron of interfering with state revenue. — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **Ellicott** suggests that Moses and Aaron having retired *re infectâ* (with the matter unresolved), Pharaoh turns to his court officers and reproaches them with allowing the Hebrews to be idle: they have time to hold meetings and listen to inflammatory harangues — why are they not kept closer to their tasks? Some change of system is requisite. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **"Make them rest"** — Ellicott corrects to "let them rest" (i.e., "you permit them to rest"). — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** notes: "Pharaoh did not reply directly to the request. Instead, he charged Moses and Aaron with an offense against the state. The Israelites were slaves of the king, and interference with their labor would in effect deprive Pharaoh of the revenues they produced. The great number of the people increased the damage done to Pharaoh's revenues." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-5.html

---

### v. 6 — "That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen…"

- **Three grades of officials.** Ellicott identifies: (1) "lords of service" (*sarey massim*, Exodus 1:11) — a small body of Egyptian superintendents; (2) "taskmasters" (*nogeshim*) — Egyptian subordinates, intermediaries; and (3) "officers" (*shoterim*, literally "scribes") — Hebrews who kept the tally of bricks. This is consonant with the bureaucratic Egyptian governmental system. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Gill** distinguishes the taskmasters as Egyptians and the officers as Israelites under them, accountable for each man's work. — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

- **Garner-Howes:** The "taskmasters" (*nogeshim*) were numerous Egyptian superintendents; the "officers" (*shoter*, "writers") were likely Hebrews who kept records of bricks produced. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-5.html

---

### vv. 7–8 — "You shall no longer supply the people with straw… require of them the same quota… For they are lazy…"

- **The role of straw in brickmaking.** Archaeology confirms that chopped straw was mixed with clay to make bricks more pliable and stronger. Straw has an acidic content (humic acid released as it decays) that binds the clay together. Bricks of all sorts have been found in Egypt — some with chopped straw, some with rough roots, some without straw at all. — Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Cole and Kaiser): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **Gill** cites Dr. Pococke's observations of an Egyptian pyramid of unburnt brick made of Nile earth "mixed up with chopped straw, in order to bind the clay together." — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

- **The burden more than doubled.** Canon Cook estimated this requirement would "more than double" the people's toils — they would have to disperse over harvest fields (often at considerable distance), detach straw from soil, gather and bundle it, and convey it to the brick-fields, then still complete the ordinary "tale." — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Pharaoh's logic:** "You seem to have enough time to make these crazy requests — then you must have enough time to work more!" — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **"Brick quotas are abundantly documented in Egypt."** — Citing Kaiser, via Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

---

### v. 9 — "Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies."

- **"Vain words" or "false words."** Ellicott says the reference is to the promises of deliverance with which Moses and Aaron had raised the people's hopes (Exodus 4:30). Pharaoh supposed these to be "vain words," as Sennacherib did those of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:20). — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Gill:** "Let them not regard words of falsehood and lies, such as were spoken by Moses and Aaron, promising them liberty and deliverance from their bondage, which he was determined never to grant." — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

---

### vv. 10–11 — The taskmasters and foremen relay Pharaoh's decree: no more straw supplied; same workload.

- **The immediate effect** of Moses' work was to make things worse for Israel, not better. Confronting evil would not be quick or easy. — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

---

### v. 12 — "So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw."

- **Stubble instead of straw.** In Egypt, reaping was done by cutting off only the ears, leaving very tall stubble in the fields. This stubble was not valued by cultivators and anyone could collect it. After gathering it and bringing it to the brick-fields, the Israelites would have to chop it small before it was fit for use. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

---

### v. 13 — "The taskmasters kept pressing them, saying, 'Fulfill your quota each day, just as you did when straw was provided.'"

- **Egyptian monuments** show foreign labourers engaged in brick-making under Egyptian overseers armed with sticks, who "haste" the labourers whenever they rest. The overseers are represented as continually saying, "Work without faintness." — Ellicott (citing Wilkinson, in Rawlinson's *Herodotus*): https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

---

### v. 14 — "The Israelite foremen… were beaten and asked, 'Why have you not fulfilled your quota… as you did before?'"

- **Beating the foremen.** This is the usual Eastern practice — when any requisition is made on a body of persons, the "head men" are alone responsible to the government and are punished if they fail to exact the full amount. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Trapp** is quoted: "Things commonly go backward with the saints before they come forward, so the corn groweth downward ere it grow upward." — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

---

### vv. 15–16 — The foremen appeal to Pharaoh: "Why are you treating your servants this way? No straw… yet we are told, 'Make bricks!' … the fault is with your own people."

- **Turning to Pharaoh, not God.** In their trouble, the children of Israel did not turn to God or Moses; they looked to Pharaoh for help. They felt that their previous bondage was better than their current increased misery. — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **Accessibility of Pharaoh.** Egyptian monarchs were accessible to all — it was part of their duty to hear complaints personally, and they typically devoted the earlier hours of each day to this (Herodotus ii.173). — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **"The fault is in thine own people"** — Ellicott says this is antithetical to the preceding clause: though the Hebrews are punished, the people really at fault are the Egyptians. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

---

### vv. 17–18 — "You are slackers! … Now get to work. You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks."

- **Idleness as a grave sin in Egypt.** Idleness was regarded by the Egyptians as one of the worst sins — it had to be specially disclaimed in the final judgment before Osiris and sometimes in tomb epitaphs. A good deal of idleness resulted from frequent religious festivals among Egyptians themselves, so the charge might seem plausible. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Pharaoh's spiritual blindness.** Garner-Howes notes: "Pharaoh regarded Moses and Aaron as trouble makers, who enticed the Hebrews by raising vain and illusive hopes. He was spiritually blind to the real import of their request." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-5.html

---

### v. 19 — "The Israelite foremen realized they were in trouble when they were told, 'You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks.'"

- **Despair sets in.** After Pharaoh confirmed the order, the officers had no hope of things getting better — they looked upon their unhappy lot as irretrievable. — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

---

### vv. 20–21 — The foremen confront Moses and Aaron: "May the LORD look upon you and judge you… you have made us a stench before Pharaoh… you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!"

- **Israel's faith dissolved quickly.** Exodus 4:31 said the people believed and worshipped; after Pharaoh's counter-attack, that faith, excitement, and worship were gone. — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **"Made our savour to be abhorred"** — literally "to stink." An idiom common to both Hebrews and Egyptians, very expressive. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **"A sword to slay us"** — Ellicott says this may not be mere Oriental hyperbole; the officers may have genuinely feared that their inability to enforce Pharaoh's impracticable demands would lead to their execution. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Whedon (Methodist):** "The bastinadoed *shoterim* have now lost all faith in Moses and Aaron, for they feel that the yoke that was to have been broken is only tightened. They forget that this is exactly what might have been expected from Jehovah's prediction (Exodus 3:19-20)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-5.html

- **Guzik** adds a spiritual application: "Satan sometimes seems friendly to us when we accept his lordship; but when we start to be free in Jesus, he often will try to make life difficult for us." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **God designed the testing.** Guzik notes that God allowed all this — in fact, designed it. God could have freed Israel without a struggle, but He knew that for them to transition from slaves to free people of the promised land, testing and stretching were absolutely necessary. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

---

### vv. 22–23 — Moses returns to the LORD: "Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me? Ever since I went to Pharaoh… You have not delivered Your people in any way."

- **Moses did right in speaking his heart to God.** G. Campbell Morgan is quoted: "Happy is the man who when he cannot understand the divine movement and, indeed, doubts it has yet faith enough in God Himself to tell Him all his doubt." — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **Moses did wrong in forgetting what God had said.** God had plainly told him in Exodus 3:19-20 that Pharaoh would not let Israel go except by a mighty hand and that God would strike Egypt with wonders. — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **"Returned unto the Lord."** Ellicott says Moses could find nothing to say to the officers — the course of events had disappointed him as much as them. All he could do was complain to God "with a freedom which seems to us almost to border on irreverence, but which God excused in him, since it had its root in his tender love for his people." The thought that he had *increased* the burdens and aggravated the misery was more than he could bear without complaining. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

- **Gill** notes that Moses "expected that God would have made a beginning as soon as he had delivered his message to Pharaoh… but, instead of that, more work was laid upon them." He adds that if Moses had called to mind Exodus 4:2 (that Pharaoh would not let the people go at first, until all the wonders were wrought), it would have relieved him. — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

- **Whedon (Methodist):** "There is a characteristic vehemence, an almost irreverent impetuosity in his prayer, most natural to the man, and yet betraying a weakness which any writer of the Jewish ages would have been glad to hide. Only Moses could have written this, and only an inspired man could write with such unworldly objectivity of himself." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-5.html

- **Constable:** "Moses' prayer of inquiry and complaint reveals the immaturity of his faith at this time. He, too, needed the demonstrations of God's power that followed." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-5.html

- **F.B. Meyer (Baptist/Holiness):** "The agony of soul through which Moses passed must have been as death to him. He died to his self-esteem, to his castle-building, to pride in his miracles, to the enthusiasm of his people, to everything that a popular leader loves. As he lay there on the ground alone before God… he was falling as a grain of wheat into the ground to die, no longer to abide alone, but to bear much fruit." — Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Meyer): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

- **God's deeper purpose.** If God were to give Moses an extended answer, it might be: "Moses, I brought trouble because I am interested in more than simply freeing Israel from slavery; I want to transform them from a slave people into a people fit for My promised land. This doesn't happen quickly or easily." — Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

---

### Tradition-Specific Notes

**Baptist View (Gill, 1746):** Gill emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty in affliction — "all afflictions are of Him, and who has always wise reasons for what He does." The purposes include: to try the faith and patience of His people; to make the Egyptians more odious to them; to make Israel more desirous of departing; and to make God's vengeance on the Egyptians appear more just and His power more manifest. — Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-5.html

**Baptist View (Garner-Howes):** Emphasizes that Pharaoh's first step was his own deliberate choice to reject knowledge of God, linking this to Romans 1:19-32 and the process of hardening. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-5.html

**Methodist/Wesleyan View (Whedon):** Notes the "strange and irreverent misconception that has led some interpreters to consider this a deceptive request" — defending that the demand was genuine and reasonable. Also emphasises the authenticity of Moses' writing: only Moses himself could have written with such "unworldly objectivity."— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-5.html

**Pentecostal/Charismatic View (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises the spiritual warfare dimension — Pharaoh as representative of the evil one, the struggle between the power of Satan and the power of God. Applies it to believers' experience of things getting worse before they get better when following God's call. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-5/

**Anglican View (Ellicott):** Dwells heavily on the historical and archaeological details — Egyptian court location, bureaucratic structure, brickmaking techniques, labour practices, local-god theology of Egypt. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/5.htm

**Dispensational/Evangelical View (Constable):** Notes five reasons God permitted the conflict: (1) to display His superior power over Pharaoh and Egypt's gods; (2) to strengthen Israel's faith; (3) to heighten anticipation of redemption; (4) to demonstrate how divine sovereignty works with human freedom; (5) that the Exodus would be forever remembered as the greatest demonstration of God's love. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-5.html

---

### Modern Scholarship Note

- **NET Bible note** (cited by Precept Austin) frames the chapter as a demonstration that "when the people of God attempt to devote their full service and allegiance to God, they encounter opposition from the world. Rather than finding instant blessing and peace, they find conflict." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-5-commentary

- **Historical labour practices:** Kenneth Kitchen's research (cited by Constable) shows that Egyptian royal workmen routinely received time off for religious observances, making Moses' request not unusual in its form — only in its object (worshipping Yahweh rather than Egyptian gods). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-5-commentary
